name: Test booster blends (Prime Male, TestoFuel)

lead: Test booster blends such as Prime Male and TestoFuel combine herbs, vitamins and minerals and are marketed to raise or support testosterone. Users hope for more muscle, energy and a leaner body composition.

Marketing says the ingredients support the body's own testosterone production or reduce its conversion or binding. No published trial of either named product was found; research on single ingredients is inconsistent, and Wikipedia states that Tribulus terrestris did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies.

paras: They are taken as daily capsules or powders bought online, usually on top of a training and diet plan. Users commonly run a bottle or two and compare energy, gym progress and bloodwork.

Supplement blends are sold without prior approval for effectiveness, and ingredients and interactions vary by product. The Australian Institute of Sport, cited by Wikipedia, discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements, citing no good evidence of effectiveness or safety.

angle.text: Test booster blends combine herbs and vitamins that are marketed to raise testosterone, for more muscle and a leaner body. They are sold online and discussed in looksmaxxing forums. No published trial of these specific products was found.

lead: Test booster blends are multi-ingredient dietary supplements marketed to raise or support testosterone, usually combining herbal extracts, vitamins and minerals. Prime Male and TestoFuel are two brands sold online. People take them hoping for the physique and energy associated with higher testosterone: more muscle, easier training recovery, leaner body composition and better drive in the gym.

The chain users describe is: ingredients nudge the body's own testosterone production or availability, training capacity improves, and muscle gain and leanness follow. Brand formulations are set by the manufacturers and change over time, so the label is the source for ingredients. Common ingredients in this product category include Tribulus terrestris, ashwagandha and fenugreek.

No published clinical trial of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products was found. Wikipedia states that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies, and its ashwagandha article notes that the herb may raise testosterone levels, with rare reports of liver injury [1].
infobox: Tribulus, ashwagandha, fenugreek, zinc, vitamin D (varies by brand)

paras: Blends differ by brand and product version, so current labels list what each contains. Tribulus terrestris has been used in supplements since the 1980s on the belief that it raises testosterone. Ashwagandha is sold as root or leaf powder or extract [1]. Fenugreek is sold as capsules, powder, tea and extract in many countries [2].

Wikipedia reports that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies and that no reviews show strength-enhancing effects. Its ashwagandha article says the herb may raise testosterone, which could matter for people on certain cancer medicines [1]. Its fenugreek article describes studies as mostly small and of limited quality and says the US FDA has not approved fenugreek for clinical use [2].

Ashwagandha has been linked to rare herb-induced liver injury, most often in people with existing liver conditions, plus diarrhea, headache, sedation and nausea; it is advised against in pregnancy and hormone-sensitive prostate cancer [1]. Fenugreek can cause digestive upset, a maple-like body odor and low blood sugar, and may interact with diabetes and anticoagulant drugs [2]. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements.
No studies found of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products.
Ingredient-level research, as summarised by Wikipedia, is inconsistent for Tribulus  and limited in quality for fenugreek [2].

Testosterone-focused forums such as T Nation discuss test boosters often. One member who used a mild booster reported worse sleep, which surprised him since zinc is a common ingredient [3]. Another posted lab results after stopping boosters and adding vitamin D and boron, reporting lower total and free testosterone [4]. Others ask whether any boosters work [5]. Such posts are individual reports.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, test boosters are discussed both as a first step before prescription therapy and as something members question.

claims.claim: Over-the-counter test boosters raise testosterone enough to help muscle gain.
Boosters made from common ingredients such as zinc improve sleep and recovery.
